topics.title: SQL basics, command categories, data types and constraints

learn.hook: SQL is the one language that banks, railways, hospitals and your school's result system all speak. You tell it WHAT you want; it works out HOW.
points: An RDBMS (relational DBMS) stores data in related tables. Popular ones: MySQL, Oracle, Microsoft SQL Server, PostgreSQL. CBSE uses MySQL.
SQL (Structured Query Language) is declarative: you state what data you want, not the steps to get it. Keywords are case-insensitive (SELECT = select), and each statement ends with a semicolon.
DDL (Data Definition Language) defines or changes structure: CREATE, ALTER, DROP. DML (Data Manipulation Language) works on the data: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE; SELECT queries the data.

Data types: CHAR(n) is fixed length: it always uses n characters, padding shorter values with spaces. VARCHAR(n) is variable length, up to n characters, using only what the value needs. INT for whole numbers, FLOAT for decimals, DATE in 'YYYY-MM-DD' format.

Constraints: NOT NULL (a value is required), UNIQUE (no duplicates), DEFAULT (a value used when none is given), PRIMARY KEY (unique and not NULL; identifies each row), FOREIGN KEY (must match a primary key in another table).

example.q: Choose data types for Aadhaar number (always 12 digits), name (up to 40 characters, length varies) and date of birth.
steps: The Aadhaar number has a fixed length and is not used in arithmetic: CHAR(12)
Date of birth: DATE, entered as 'YYYY-MM-DD'

learn.reallife: A bank's accounts table might make the account number the PRIMARY KEY and declare the balance column NOT NULL, so no two accounts share a number and no account is left without a balance.

games.title: Match the constraint to its rule
pairs: No two rows may share a value
Value used when none is given
Unique and not NULL, identifies each row
Must match a key in another table

quiz.q: Which of these is a DDL command?
quiz.explain: ALTER changes the structure of a table, so it is DDL. INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE work on the data (DML).
quiz.mistake: Thinks any command that changes something is DDL

quiz.q: Which of these is a DML command?
quiz.explain: UPDATE changes data inside a table, which is data manipulation.
quiz.mistake: Confuses changing data with changing structure

quiz.q: A column is declared CHAR(10). How many characters of storage does the value 'Ram' take in that column?
quiz.explain: CHAR(n) is fixed length, so the value is padded with spaces to 10 characters.
quiz.mistake: Treats CHAR like VARCHAR

quiz.q: Which data type should store students' names whose lengths vary from 3 to 30 characters, without wasting space?
quiz.explain: VARCHAR(30) stores only as many characters as each name needs, up to 30.
quiz.mistake: Uses fixed-length CHAR for variable data

quiz.q: In which format is a DATE value written in MySQL?
quiz.explain: MySQL dates are entered as 'YYYY-MM-DD', for example '2026-03-15'.
quiz.mistake: Uses the everyday Indian date format

quiz.q: Which constraint makes MySQL use a given value automatically when an INSERT does not supply one for that column?
quiz.explain: DEFAULT supplies a value, such as DEFAULT 'Delhi', when none is given.
quiz.mistake: Confuses DEFAULT with NOT NULL

quiz.q: Which statement about SQL is TRUE?
options: SQL is a declarative language: you say what data you want, not how to get it
Every SQL statement must start with CREATE
SQL can be used only with Oracle
quiz.explain: SQL is declarative and its keywords are case-insensitive; it works with MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL and others.
quiz.mistake: Thinks SQL keywords must be written in capitals

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A PRIMARY KEY column cannot contain duplicate values.
Reason (R): A PRIMARY KEY combines the UNIQUE and NOT NULL rules.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Because a primary key must be unique (and not NULL), duplicates are rejected. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks primary keys only forbid NULL

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What's the difference between DDL and DML?'
teach.praise: Superb! DDL defines or changes the structure (CREATE, ALTER, DROP), while DML works with the data (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE).
teach.nudge: Which category changes the table's structure, and which changes the rows inside?

topics.title: Data definition: CREATE, USE, DESCRIBE, ALTER and DROP

learn.hook: Before a single record goes in, someone has to build the shelves. DDL is SQL's carpentry.
points: Databases: CREATE DATABASE School; SHOW DATABASES; USE School; (selects it for use) DROP DATABASE School; (deletes it and all its tables).
CREATE TABLE STUDENT (RollNo INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL, Class INT, City VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'Delhi'); SHOW TABLES; lists the tables in the current database.
DESCRIBE STUDENT; or DESC STUDENT; shows the structure: column names, data types, NULL allowed or not, keys and defaults.
ALTER TABLE changes structure: ADD Phone CHAR(10); DROP Phone; ADD PRIMARY KEY (RollNo); DROP PRIMARY KEY; ADD FOREIGN KEY (ClassID) REFERENCES CLASS(ClassID); MODIFY Name VARCHAR(40);
DROP TABLE STUDENT; removes the table completely: its structure and its data. DELETE FROM STUDENT; (DML) removes only the rows and leaves the empty table.

example.q: Add a column Email of type VARCHAR(50) to the table STUDENT, then view the new structure.
steps: ALTER TABLE STUDENT ADD Email VARCHAR(50);
example.answer: ALTER TABLE STUDENT ADD Email VARCHAR(50); then DESC STUDENT;

learn.reallife: When a hospital decides to start recording each patient's ABHA health ID, the database team runs an ALTER TABLE ... ADD statement rather than rebuilding the whole patient table.

games.title: Set up a new database
games.prompt: In the order you run the commands

games.title: Match the task to the command
pairs: Select a database to work in

quiz.q: Which command makes the database School the current database?
quiz.explain: USE databasename; selects a database so that later commands work inside it.
quiz.mistake: Invents an OPEN command

quiz.q: Which command shows the structure (columns, types, keys) of the table STUDENT?
quiz.explain: DESCRIBE or DESC shows a table's structure.
quiz.mistake: Confuses viewing structure with viewing data

quiz.q: Which statement correctly adds a column Phone of type CHAR(10) to the table STUDENT?
options: ALTER TABLE STUDENT ADD Phone CHAR(10);
quiz.explain: Adding a column changes the structure, so it needs ALTER TABLE ... ADD.
quiz.mistake: Uses UPDATE or INSERT for structural changes

quiz.q: Which statement increases the size of the column Name in STUDENT to VARCHAR(50)?
options: ALTER TABLE STUDENT ADD Name VARCHAR(50);
ALTER TABLE STUDENT MODIFY Name VARCHAR(50);
quiz.explain: MODIFY within ALTER TABLE changes an existing column's definition.
quiz.mistake: Uses ADD, which would try to create a second Name column

quiz.q: What is the difference between DROP TABLE STUDENT; and DELETE FROM STUDENT;?
options: DROP removes the table's structure and data; DELETE removes only the rows
DELETE removes the structure; DROP removes the rows
quiz.explain: DROP is DDL and removes the whole table. DELETE is DML and leaves an empty table behind.
quiz.mistake: Thinks DELETE also removes the table

quiz.q: Which statement makes RollNo the primary key of an existing table STUDENT?
options: ALTER TABLE STUDENT ADD PRIMARY KEY (RollNo);
ALTER TABLE STUDENT MODIFY KEY RollNo;
UPDATE STUDENT SET PRIMARY KEY = RollNo;
quiz.explain: ALTER TABLE ... ADD PRIMARY KEY (column) adds the constraint.
quiz.mistake: Tries to set a key using UPDATE

quiz.q: Which clause in CREATE TABLE makes ClassID in STUDENT refer to the ClassID column of the CLASS table?
quiz.explain: FOREIGN KEY (column) REFERENCES table(column) creates the link.
quiz.mistake: Confuses foreign key syntax with primary key syntax

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): After DROP TABLE STUDENT;, the command DESC STUDENT; gives an error.
Reason (R): DROP TABLE removes the table's structure as well as its data.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: With the structure gone, there is no table to describe. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks DROP removes only the rows

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If I want to get rid of a table, should I use DROP or DELETE?'
teach.praise: Exactly! DROP TABLE removes the whole table, structure and all; DELETE removes only the rows and keeps the table.
teach.nudge: Which command removes the table itself, and which only empties it?

topics.title: Data manipulation: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE

learn.hook: Forget the WHERE clause in an UPDATE and every employee in the company gets the same salary. Ask any database admin about their worst day.
points: INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES (101, 'Asha', 12, 'Pune'); gives values for every column, in the table's column order.
INSERT INTO STUDENT (RollNo, Name) VALUES (102, 'Ravi'); gives values only for the listed columns; the others get NULL or their DEFAULT. Text and dates go in single quotes.
With foreign keys, insert into the referenced (parent) table first. A STUDENT row with ClassID 12 is rejected unless CLASS already has ClassID 12.
UPDATE STUDENT SET City = 'Agra' WHERE RollNo = 101; changes matching rows. Without WHERE, every row is updated. UPDATE changes data (DML); ALTER changes structure (DDL).
DELETE FROM STUDENT WHERE RollNo = 101; removes matching rows. Without WHERE, all rows are deleted, but the empty table remains.

example.q: Give every employee in the IT department a 10% raise in the table EMP(EmpID, Name, Dept, Salary).
steps: Use UPDATE, because it changes existing data
WHERE Dept = 'IT' limits it to IT
example.answer: UPDATE EMP SET Salary = Salary * 1.10 WHERE Dept = 'IT';

learn.reallife: When the government revises dearness allowance, payroll teams run a single UPDATE with a WHERE clause instead of editing lakhs of salary records by hand.

games.title: DML facts
items: UPDATE without a WHERE clause changes every row.
No condition means all rows match.
DELETE FROM STUDENT; removes the table's structure.
It deletes the rows only; the empty table remains.
ALTER changes data and UPDATE changes structure.
It is the reverse: ALTER changes structure, UPDATE changes data.
Text values are written in single quotes in INSERT.
A child row with a foreign key should be inserted before its parent row exists.
The parent row must exist first.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly inserts a row with only RollNo 7 and Name 'Isha' into STUDENT(RollNo, Name, Class, City)?
quiz.explain: When values are given for only some columns, those columns must be listed.
quiz.mistake: Omits the column list while supplying fewer values than columns

quiz.q: Table EMP has rows for Asha (HR), Ravi (IT), Meena (IT) and Kabir (Sales). After DELETE FROM EMP WHERE Dept = 'IT';, how many rows remain?
quiz.explain: The two IT rows (Ravi, Meena) are deleted, leaving Asha and Kabir.
quiz.mistake: Deletes everything, forgetting the WHERE clause

quiz.q: What happens when UPDATE EMP SET Salary = 30000; is run?
options: An error occurs because WHERE is missing
quiz.explain: Without WHERE, UPDATE applies to every row of the table.
quiz.mistake: Thinks WHERE is compulsory in UPDATE

quiz.q: Tables CLASS(ClassID primary key) and STUDENT(RollNo, ClassID foreign key referencing CLASS). In which order should the first records be inserted?
quiz.explain: A student's ClassID must already exist in CLASS, so the parent table is filled first.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the foreign-key dependency

quiz.q: Which statement changes Ravi's city to 'Indore' in EMP(EmpID, Name, City), where Ravi's EmpID is 2?
options: ALTER TABLE EMP SET City = 'Indore' WHERE EmpID = 2;
UPDATE EMP SET City = 'Indore' WHERE EmpID = 2;
quiz.explain: UPDATE ... SET ... WHERE changes data in existing rows.
quiz.mistake: Uses ALTER for a data change or forgets SET

quiz.q: What is the difference between ALTER and UPDATE?
options: ALTER changes the table's structure; UPDATE changes the data in rows
ALTER changes data; UPDATE changes structure
quiz.explain: ALTER is DDL (structure), UPDATE is DML (data).
quiz.mistake: Swaps the roles of ALTER and UPDATE

quiz.q: Table PRODUCT has 50 rows. After DELETE FROM PRODUCT; what is true?
options: The table exists but has 0 rows
Only the first row is deleted
quiz.explain: DELETE without WHERE removes all rows but keeps the table structure.
quiz.mistake: Confuses DELETE with DROP

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES (11, 'Neel'); fails when STUDENT has four columns.
Reason (R): Without a column list, INSERT must provide a value for every column.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Only two values are given for four columns, so MySQL reports a column count mismatch. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks missing values are filled in automatically without a column list

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What's the danger of writing an UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause?'
teach.praise: Exactly! Without WHERE, UPDATE and DELETE affect every row, so always add a condition.
teach.nudge: Which rows are affected when there is no condition?

topics.title: SELECT: columns, aliases, computed columns and DISTINCT

learn.hook: SELECT is the most-used SQL word on the planet. Every app that shows you a list, from Zomato's menus to your exam timetable, runs one.
points: SELECT * FROM EMP; shows all columns. SELECT Name, City FROM EMP; shows only the chosen columns, in the order you list them.
Computed columns: SELECT Name, Salary * 12 FROM EMP; works out a value for each row without changing the stored data.
Column alias with AS: SELECT Name, Salary * 12 AS AnnualSalary FROM EMP; renames the column heading in the output. An alias containing spaces goes in quotes: AS "Annual Salary".
DISTINCT removes duplicate values from the output: SELECT DISTINCT City FROM EMP; lists each city once.
SELECT never changes the table: it only displays a result.

example.q: From EMP(Name, Dept, Salary, City) with cities Delhi, Pune, Delhi, Mumbai, Pune, Delhi, list each city once.
steps: Duplicates must go, so use DISTINCT
Result: Delhi, Pune and Mumbai (3 rows)
example.answer: SELECT DISTINCT City FROM EMP; gives 3 rows

learn.reallife: A food-delivery app shows each cuisine once in its filter menu even though thousands of restaurants serve it: that is a DISTINCT query.

games.title: Match the query to what it does
pairs: SELECT Name AS Employee FROM EMP;

games.title: SELECT facts
items: SELECT * displays every column of the table.
SELECT Salary * 2 FROM EMP; doubles the salaries stored in the table.
It only displays doubled values; the data is unchanged.
An alias changes the column's name permanently in the table.
It only renames the heading in the output.
DISTINCT removes duplicate values from the result.
An alias containing a space must be enclosed in quotes.

quiz.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary, City): Asha HR 40000 Delhi; Ravi IT 55000 Pune; Meena IT 60000 Delhi; Kabir Sales 35000 Mumbai; Zoya HR NULL Pune; Dev IT 50000 Delhi. How many rows does SELECT DISTINCT City FROM EMP; return?
quiz.explain: The distinct cities are Delhi, Pune and Mumbai.
quiz.mistake: Counts all rows instead of unique values

quiz.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary, City): Asha HR 40000 Delhi; Ravi IT 55000 Pune; Meena IT 60000 Delhi; Kabir Sales 35000 Mumbai; Zoya HR NULL Pune; Dev IT 50000 Delhi. How many rows does SELECT DISTINCT Dept FROM EMP; return?
quiz.explain: The departments are HR, IT and Sales; each appears once in the output.
quiz.mistake: Counts every row instead of unique departments

quiz.q: Which query displays only the Name and City columns of EMP?
quiz.explain: List the required columns, separated by commas, after SELECT.
quiz.mistake: Uses * when only some columns are wanted

quiz.q: What does SELECT Name, Salary * 12 AS Annual FROM EMP; display?
options: An error, because Annual is not a column of EMP
Each name with twelve times the salary, under the heading Annual
The salaries are permanently multiplied by 12
quiz.explain: Salary * 12 is computed for each row and AS gives it the heading Annual. The table is unchanged.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a computed column changes the stored data

quiz.q: Which query renames the Name column to 'Student Name' in the output?
options: SELECT Name AS "Student Name" FROM STUDENT;
SELECT Name AS Student Name FROM STUDENT;
quiz.explain: An alias containing a space must be in quotes after AS.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the quotes around an alias that has a space

quiz.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary): Asha HR 40000; Ravi IT 55000; Meena IT 60000; Kabir Sales 35000; Zoya HR NULL; Dev IT 50000. What is the highest value shown by SELECT Name, Salary + 5000 FROM EMP;?
quiz.explain: The computed column adds 5000 to each salary; the highest salary is 60000, so 65000 is shown for Meena.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the computation and reads the stored value

quiz.q: What does SELECT DISTINCT Dept, City FROM EMP; return?
options: Each distinct combination of Dept and City
quiz.explain: With several columns, DISTINCT removes rows whose combination of values repeats.
quiz.mistake: Thinks DISTINCT applies only to the first column

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Running SELECT on a table does not change the data in it.
Reason (R): SELECT only retrieves and displays data.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: SELECT is a query; it reads data and shows a result without modifying the table. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks computed columns in SELECT update the table

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I list each city only once, even if many rows have the same city?'
teach.praise: Spot on! SELECT DISTINCT City removes duplicates so each city appears once.
teach.nudge: Which keyword removes repeated values from the output?

topics.title: WHERE with operators, BETWEEN, IN and NULL

learn.hook: WHERE Salary = NULL looks right but returns nothing, every single time. NULL plays by its own rules.
points: WHERE filters rows using relational operators (=, <, >, <=, >=, <> or !=), logical operators (AND, OR, NOT) and arithmetic in conditions (e.g. WHERE Salary * 12 > 600000).
BETWEEN a AND b selects values in a range, including both ends: WHERE Salary BETWEEN 40000 AND 55000 includes 40000 and 55000.
IN checks membership in a list: WHERE City IN ('Delhi', 'Pune'). NOT IN selects values outside the list.
NULL means unknown, so = NULL and <> NULL are never true. Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL: WHERE Salary IS NULL.
AND is evaluated before OR; use brackets to make your meaning clear.

example.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary, City): Asha HR 40000 Delhi; Ravi IT 55000 Pune; Meena IT 60000 Delhi; Kabir Sales 35000 Mumbai; Zoya HR NULL Pune; Dev IT 50000 Delhi. Which names does SELECT Name FROM EMP WHERE City = 'Delhi' AND Salary > 45000; show?

learn.reallife: A bank's fraud desk might query WHERE Amount > 100000 AND City NOT IN ('Mumbai', 'Delhi') to spot unusual high-value transactions.

items.text: WHERE Salary IS ___ finds rows with no salary
WHERE NOT City = 'Pune' is the same as WHERE City ___ 'Pune'

games.title: Filter facts
items: BETWEEN is inclusive at both ends.
WHERE Salary = NULL finds rows whose salary is NULL.
Use IS NULL; comparing with = NULL is never true.
City IN ('A', 'B') is equivalent to City = 'A' OR City = 'B'.
IN tests membership in the list.
NOT IN ('Delhi') selects rows whose city is not Delhi.
AND has lower precedence than OR.

quiz.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary): Asha HR 40000; Ravi IT 55000; Meena IT 60000; Kabir Sales 35000; Zoya HR NULL; Dev IT 50000. How many rows does SELECT * FROM EMP WHERE Salary BETWEEN 40000 AND 55000; return?
quiz.explain: BETWEEN is inclusive: 40000 (Asha), 55000 (Ravi) and 50000 (Dev). Zoya's NULL is not in any range.
quiz.mistake: Excludes the boundary values 40000 and 55000

quiz.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary, City): Asha HR 40000 Delhi; Ravi IT 55000 Pune; Meena IT 60000 Delhi; Kabir Sales 35000 Mumbai; Zoya HR NULL Pune; Dev IT 50000 Delhi. How many rows does SELECT * FROM EMP WHERE City IN ('Pune', 'Mumbai'); return?
quiz.explain: Pune: Ravi and Zoya; Mumbai: Kabir. That makes 3 rows.
quiz.mistake: Counts only one of the listed cities

quiz.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary): Asha HR 40000; Ravi IT 55000; Meena IT 60000; Kabir Sales 35000; Zoya HR NULL; Dev IT 50000. Which name does SELECT Name FROM EMP WHERE Salary IS NULL; show?
quiz.explain: Only Zoya's salary is NULL. IS NULL is the right way to test for it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks NULL rows cannot be selected at all

quiz.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary): Asha HR 40000; Ravi IT 55000; Meena IT 60000; Kabir Sales 35000; Zoya HR NULL; Dev IT 50000. How many rows does SELECT * FROM EMP WHERE Salary = NULL; return?
quiz.explain: A comparison with NULL using = is never true, so no rows are returned. IS NULL would find Zoya.
quiz.mistake: Treats = NULL like IS NULL

quiz.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary): Asha HR 40000; Ravi IT 55000; Meena IT 60000; Kabir Sales 35000; Zoya HR NULL; Dev IT 50000. How many rows does SELECT * FROM EMP WHERE Dept = 'IT' OR Salary < 40000; return?
quiz.explain: IT gives Ravi, Meena and Dev; Salary < 40000 adds Kabir. 3 + 1 = 4 rows.
quiz.mistake: Uses AND instead of OR, or double-counts

quiz.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary, City): Asha HR 40000 Delhi; Ravi IT 55000 Pune; Meena IT 60000 Delhi; Kabir Sales 35000 Mumbai; Zoya HR NULL Pune; Dev IT 50000 Delhi. How many rows does SELECT * FROM EMP WHERE City NOT IN ('Delhi'); return?
quiz.explain: Cities other than Delhi are Pune (Ravi, Zoya) and Mumbai (Kabir).
quiz.mistake: Counts the Delhi rows instead

quiz.q: Which query lists employees whose annual salary (Salary * 12) is more than 600000?
options: SELECT * FROM EMP WHERE Salary * 12 IS 600000;
quiz.explain: Salary * 12 is the annual salary, and arithmetic can be used inside a WHERE condition on each row. Salary > 600000 tests the monthly salary, and IS works only with NULL.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies on the wrong side of the comparison

quiz.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary): Asha HR 40000; Ravi IT 55000; Meena IT 60000; Kabir Sales 35000; Zoya HR NULL; Dev IT 50000. How many rows does SELECT * FROM EMP WHERE Dept = 'HR' AND Salary IS NOT NULL; return?
quiz.explain: HR has Asha (40000) and Zoya (NULL); only Asha has a non-NULL salary.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to exclude the NULL salary

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I find rows where a value is missing (NULL)?'
teach.praise: Perfect! Use IS NULL, because comparing with = NULL is never true.
teach.nudge: Which special operator tests for NULL, and why does = NULL fail?

topics.title: Pattern matching with LIKE and sorting with ORDER BY

learn.hook: Find every customer whose name starts with 'S' and list them from the highest bill down: two tiny clauses, LIKE and ORDER BY, do it.
points: LIKE matches text patterns using two wildcards: % stands for any number of characters (including none), and _ stands for exactly one character.
'A%' starts with A; '%a' ends with a; '%an%' contains 'an'; '_a%' has a as the second letter; '____' (four underscores) is exactly four characters long. NOT LIKE excludes a pattern.
ORDER BY sorts the result: ORDER BY Salary; is ascending (ASC, the default) and ORDER BY Salary DESC; is descending.
Sorting on several columns: ORDER BY Dept, Salary DESC; sorts by Dept first and, within each department, by Salary from high to low.
ORDER BY comes after WHERE in a query: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... ORDER BY ...;

example.q: From EMP, list the names starting with 'M' or ending with 'a', in alphabetical order. (Names: Asha, Ravi, Meena, Kabir, Zoya, Dev.)
steps: WHERE Name LIKE 'M%' OR Name LIKE '%a'
'M%' matches Meena; '%a' matches Asha, Meena and Zoya
ORDER BY Name sorts them alphabetically

learn.reallife: When you type 'Pan' in a railway station search box, the app may run something like WHERE StationName LIKE 'Pan%' to suggest Panvel and Panipat.

games.title: Match the pattern to its meaning

quiz.q: Names in EMP: Asha, Ravi, Meena, Kabir, Zoya, Dev. Which names does SELECT Name FROM EMP WHERE Name LIKE '%a'; return?
quiz.explain: '%a' means the name ends with a: Asha, Meena and Zoya.
quiz.mistake: Reads '%a' as 'contains a'

quiz.q: Names in EMP: Asha, Ravi, Meena, Kabir, Zoya, Dev. How many names does WHERE Name LIKE '_a%' match?
quiz.explain: '_a%' needs a as the second letter: Ravi and Kabir.
quiz.mistake: Reads _ as any number of characters

quiz.q: Which pattern matches names that are exactly 4 characters long?
quiz.explain: Each _ matches exactly one character, so four underscores match exactly four characters.
quiz.mistake: Uses % for a fixed number of characters

quiz.q: Which query lists employees from the highest salary to the lowest?
options: SELECT * FROM EMP ORDER Salary DOWN;
SELECT * FROM EMP ORDER BY Salary;
SELECT * FROM EMP SORT BY Salary DESC;
SELECT * FROM EMP ORDER BY Salary DESC;
quiz.explain: DESC gives descending order. Without it, ORDER BY sorts in ascending order.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the default order is ascending

quiz.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary): Asha HR 40000; Ravi IT 55000; Meena IT 60000; Kabir Sales 35000; Zoya HR NULL; Dev IT 50000. Whose name comes first in the output of SELECT Name FROM EMP WHERE Salary IS NOT NULL ORDER BY Salary;?
quiz.explain: Ascending order puts the lowest salary first: Kabir with 35000.
quiz.mistake: Assumes ORDER BY sorts in descending order by default

quiz.q: What does ORDER BY Dept, Salary DESC do?
options: Sorts by Salary first, then Dept
Gives an error because two columns are listed
Sorts by Dept ascending, and within each Dept by Salary descending
quiz.explain: The first column is the main sort (ascending by default); DESC applies only to Salary.
quiz.mistake: Thinks DESC applies to every column in the list

quiz.q: Which query finds products whose name contains the word 'pen' anywhere?
quiz.explain: % on both sides allows any characters before and after 'pen'. = does not use wildcards.
quiz.mistake: Uses = with wildcards

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): WHERE Name LIKE 'R%' matches 'Ravi' and 'R'.
Reason (R): % matches zero or more characters.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: 'R%' needs R first followed by any number of characters, including none, so both match. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks % must match at least one character

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'In LIKE patterns, what's the difference between % and _?'
teach.praise: Excellent! % matches any number of characters (even none), while _ matches exactly one character.
teach.nudge: How many characters does each wildcard stand for?

learn.hook: COUNT(*) and COUNT(Salary) can give different answers on the same table. The difference is one NULL, and it is a favourite board question.
points: Single-row functions work on each row separately and return one value per row (e.g. UPPER(Name)); you only need to know this difference, because single-row functions are not in the CBSE CS exam syllabus. Aggregate (multi-row) functions work on a group of rows and return one value for the whole group.
Aggregates: MAX(col) largest value, MIN(col) smallest, SUM(col) total, AVG(col) average, COUNT(col) number of non-NULL values in the column.
COUNT(*) counts all rows, including rows with NULLs. COUNT(col) skips NULLs. COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts the different non-NULL values.
SUM, AVG, MAX and MIN ignore NULL values. So AVG(col) = SUM(col) / COUNT(col), not divided by COUNT(*).
Aggregates can be combined with WHERE: SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM EMP WHERE Dept = 'IT'; averages only the IT rows.

example.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary): Asha HR 40000; Ravi IT 55000; Meena IT 60000; Kabir Sales 35000; Zoya HR NULL; Dev IT 50000. Find COUNT(*), COUNT(Salary), SUM(Salary) and AVG(Salary).

learn.reallife: At the end of an IPL season, the stats team runs MAX(Runs) for the Orange Cap, SUM(Runs) for team totals and AVG for batting averages, all aggregate functions.

games.title: Match the function to its result on salaries 40000, 55000, 60000, 35000, NULL, 50000

quiz.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary): Asha HR 40000; Ravi IT 55000; Meena IT 60000; Kabir Sales 35000; Zoya HR NULL; Dev IT 50000. What does SELECT COUNT(*) FROM EMP; return?
quiz.explain: COUNT(*) counts every row, including the row where Salary is NULL.
quiz.mistake: Thinks COUNT(*) skips rows containing NULL

quiz.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary): Asha HR 40000; Ravi IT 55000; Meena IT 60000; Kabir Sales 35000; Zoya HR NULL; Dev IT 50000. What does SELECT COUNT(Salary) FROM EMP; return?
quiz.explain: COUNT(column) counts only non-NULL values; Zoya's NULL is skipped.
quiz.mistake: Treats COUNT(Salary) like COUNT(*)

quiz.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary): Asha HR 40000; Ravi IT 55000; Meena IT 60000; Kabir Sales 35000; Zoya HR NULL; Dev IT 50000. What does SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM EMP; return?
quiz.explain: AVG ignores the NULL: 240000 / 5 = 48000.
quiz.mistake: Divides by all 6 rows, giving 40000

quiz.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary): Asha HR 40000; Ravi IT 55000; Meena IT 60000; Kabir Sales 35000; Zoya HR NULL; Dev IT 50000. What does SELECT MAX(Salary) - MIN(Salary) FROM EMP; return?
quiz.explain: MAX is 60000 and MIN is 35000 (NULL is ignored). 60000 - 35000 = 25000.
quiz.mistake: Treats NULL as 0 and takes 0 as the minimum

quiz.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary): Asha HR 40000; Ravi IT 55000; Meena IT 60000; Kabir Sales 35000; Zoya HR NULL; Dev IT 50000. What does SELECT SUM(Salary) FROM EMP WHERE Dept = 'IT'; return?
quiz.explain: The IT salaries are 55000, 60000 and 50000, totalling 165000.
quiz.mistake: Misses one of the IT rows

quiz.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary): Asha HR 40000; Ravi IT 55000; Meena IT 60000; Kabir Sales 35000; Zoya HR NULL; Dev IT 50000. What does SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT Dept) FROM EMP; return?
quiz.explain: The different departments are HR, IT and Sales.
quiz.mistake: Counts all rows instead of distinct values

quiz.q: Which of these is an aggregate (multi-row) function?
quiz.explain: AVG works on many rows and returns one value; the others return a value for each row.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any built-in function is an aggregate

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): For a column with some NULL values, AVG(col) may differ from SUM(col) / COUNT(*).
Reason (R): AVG ignores NULL values, but COUNT(*) counts every row.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: AVG divides by the number of non-NULL values; COUNT(*) includes NULL rows, so the results differ. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks aggregates treat NULL as zero

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why do COUNT(*) and COUNT(Salary) give different answers on my table?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! COUNT(*) counts every row, while COUNT(Salary) skips the rows where Salary is NULL.
teach.nudge: What does each COUNT do with rows that have NULL in Salary?

learn.hook: 'Total sales per region', 'average marks per section', 'number of trains per zone': every 'per' in a question is a hint to use GROUP BY.
points: GROUP BY col puts rows with the same value of col into one group; aggregate functions then give one result per group: SELECT Dept, COUNT(*) FROM EMP GROUP BY Dept;
Columns in the SELECT list should be either the grouping column(s) or aggregates.
HAVING filters groups after grouping, using aggregate conditions: ... GROUP BY Dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
WHERE filters individual rows BEFORE grouping and cannot use aggregate functions; HAVING filters groups AFTER grouping.
Clause order: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... GROUP BY ... HAVING ... ORDER BY ...;

example.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary): Asha HR 40000; Ravi IT 55000; Meena IT 60000; Kabir Sales 35000; Zoya HR NULL; Dev IT 50000. Find the number of employees and total salary in each department.
steps: SELECT Dept, COUNT(*), SUM(Salary) FROM EMP GROUP BY Dept;

learn.reallife: Indian Railways can report punctuality by zone with GROUP BY Zone and then use HAVING AVG(Delay) > 30 to flag only the zones that need attention.

games.title: Clause order in a SELECT query

quiz.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary): Asha HR 40000; Ravi IT 55000; Meena IT 60000; Kabir Sales 35000; Zoya HR NULL; Dev IT 50000. How many rows does SELECT Dept, COUNT(*) FROM EMP GROUP BY Dept; return?
quiz.explain: One row per department: HR, IT and Sales.
quiz.mistake: Thinks GROUP BY returns every original row

quiz.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary): Asha HR 40000; Ravi IT 55000; Meena IT 60000; Kabir Sales 35000; Zoya HR NULL; Dev IT 50000. In SELECT Dept, COUNT(*) FROM EMP GROUP BY Dept;, what count is shown for IT?
quiz.explain: Ravi, Meena and Dev are in IT.
quiz.mistake: Miscounts the rows in the group

quiz.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary): Asha HR 40000; Ravi IT 55000; Meena IT 60000; Kabir Sales 35000; Zoya HR NULL; Dev IT 50000. Which departments does SELECT Dept FROM EMP GROUP BY Dept HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2; return?
quiz.explain: HR has 2 rows and IT has 3, while Sales has only 1.
quiz.mistake: Uses COUNT(Salary) and drops HR because of Zoya's NULL

quiz.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary): Asha HR 40000; Ravi IT 55000; Meena IT 60000; Kabir Sales 35000; Zoya HR NULL; Dev IT 50000. In SELECT Dept, AVG(Salary) FROM EMP GROUP BY Dept;, what average is shown for HR?
quiz.explain: HR salaries are 40000 and NULL. AVG ignores NULL, so the average is 40000 / 1 = 40000.
quiz.mistake: Treats NULL as 0 and divides by 2

quiz.q: Which query lists the departments whose total salary is more than 100000?
options: SELECT Dept FROM EMP GROUP BY Dept HAVING SUM(Salary) > 100000;
SELECT Dept FROM EMP WHERE SUM(Salary) > 100000 GROUP BY Dept;
SELECT Dept FROM EMP GROUP BY SUM(Salary) > 100000;
SELECT Dept FROM EMP HAVING Salary > 100000;
quiz.explain: A condition on an aggregate must go in HAVING, after GROUP BY. WHERE cannot use SUM().
quiz.mistake: Puts an aggregate condition in WHERE

quiz.q: What is the main difference between WHERE and HAVING?
options: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after grouping
WHERE filters groups; HAVING filters rows
HAVING can only be used without GROUP BY
quiz.explain: WHERE works on individual rows and HAVING works on the groups made by GROUP BY.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the roles of WHERE and HAVING

quiz.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary, City): Asha HR 40000 Delhi; Ravi IT 55000 Pune; Meena IT 60000 Delhi; Kabir Sales 35000 Mumbai; Zoya HR NULL Pune; Dev IT 50000 Delhi. How many rows does SELECT City, COUNT(*) FROM EMP WHERE Dept = 'IT' GROUP BY City; return?
quiz.explain: WHERE keeps Ravi (Pune), Meena (Delhi) and Dev (Delhi); grouping by city gives Delhi and Pune.
quiz.mistake: Groups before filtering, or forgets that two IT employees share a city

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): SELECT Dept, SUM(Salary) FROM EMP WHERE SUM(Salary) > 50000 GROUP BY Dept; gives an error.
Reason (R): Aggregate functions cannot be used in a WHERE clause.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: WHERE is applied to single rows before groups exist, so SUM() is not allowed there; the condition belongs in HAVING. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks WHERE and HAVING are interchangeable

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'When do I use HAVING instead of WHERE?'
teach.praise: Excellent! HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and can use aggregates; WHERE filters rows before grouping.
teach.nudge: Which one works on groups and can use functions like COUNT or SUM?

topics.title: Cartesian product and joins on two tables

learn.hook: Student names live in one table and class teachers in another. A join brings them together, and the degree-and-cardinality question about it is almost guaranteed in the board paper.
points: Cartesian product (cross join): every row of the first table is paired with every row of the second. Degree = degree1 + degree2; cardinality = cardinality1 × cardinality2. In SQL: SELECT * FROM STUDENT, CLASS;

Equi-join: keep only the pairs where the common attribute is equal: SELECT * FROM STUDENT, CLASS WHERE STUDENT.ClassID = CLASS.ClassID; or ... FROM STUDENT JOIN CLASS ON STUDENT.ClassID = CLASS.ClassID; The common column appears twice in the output.
Natural join: SELECT * FROM STUDENT NATURAL JOIN CLASS; joins on the common column(s) and shows that column only once.

Table aliases shorten queries and remove ambiguity: SELECT S.Name, C.Teacher FROM STUDENT S, CLASS C WHERE S.ClassID = C.ClassID; A column name found in both tables must be qualified with its table name or alias.
Exam tasks: write queries on given tables, predict query output, create tables with constraints, and differentiate commands (WHERE vs HAVING, DELETE vs DROP, CHAR vs VARCHAR).

example.q: STUDENT(RollNo, Name, ClassID) has 3 rows: (1, Anu, 11), (2, Bilal, 12), (3, Chitra, 11). CLASS(ClassID, Teacher) has 2 rows: (11, Mr Rao), (12, Ms Iyer). Find the degree and cardinality of STUDENT × CLASS, and the rows of the equi-join.
steps: The equi-join keeps the pairs with equal ClassID: Anu–Mr Rao, Bilal–Ms Iyer, Chitra–Mr Rao
example.answer: Cartesian product: degree 5, cardinality 6; equi-join: 3 rows

learn.reallife: An online shopping site keeps ORDERS and CUSTOMERS in separate tables and joins them on CustomerID whenever it prints a delivery label with your name and address.

items.q: Degree of A(3 cols) × B(4 cols)
Cardinality of A(5 rows) × B(4 rows)
Degree of P(2 cols) × Q(2 cols)
Cardinality of P(10 rows) × Q(3 rows)
Degree of X(5 cols) × Y(1 col)

games.title: Match the join to its description
pairs: Every row paired with every row
Pairs with equal common values; common column shown twice
Joins on the common column and shows it once
Short name such as S for STUDENT

quiz.q: Table A has 4 columns and 6 rows; table B has 3 columns and 5 rows. What is the degree of A × B?
quiz.explain: Degree of a Cartesian product = 4 + 3 = 7.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the degrees

quiz.q: Table A has 4 columns and 6 rows; table B has 3 columns and 5 rows. What is the cardinality of A × B?
quiz.explain: Cardinality of a Cartesian product = 6 × 5 = 30.
quiz.mistake: Adds the cardinalities

quiz.q: STUDENT(RollNo, Name, ClassID) has rows (1, Anu, 11), (2, Bilal, 12), (3, Chitra, 11); CLASS(ClassID, Teacher) has (11, Mr Rao), (12, Ms Iyer). How many rows does SELECT * FROM STUDENT, CLASS; return?
quiz.explain: Without a join condition, every student is paired with every class: 3 × 2 = 6.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the tables are matched on ClassID automatically

quiz.q: STUDENT(RollNo, Name, ClassID): (1, Anu, 11), (2, Bilal, 12), (3, Chitra, 11). CLASS(ClassID, Teacher): (11, Mr Rao), (12, Ms Iyer). Which names does SELECT S.Name FROM STUDENT S, CLASS C WHERE S.ClassID = C.ClassID AND C.Teacher = 'Mr Rao'; show?
quiz.explain: The equi-join pairs each student with their class; Mr Rao teaches class 11, which has Anu and Chitra.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the join condition or the teacher filter

quiz.q: STUDENT(RollNo, Name, ClassID) and CLASS(ClassID, Teacher). How many columns does SELECT * FROM STUDENT NATURAL JOIN CLASS; display?
quiz.explain: A natural join shows the common column ClassID only once: RollNo, Name, ClassID and Teacher.
quiz.mistake: Counts ClassID twice, as in an equi-join

quiz.q: Why does SELECT Name, ClassID FROM STUDENT, CLASS WHERE STUDENT.ClassID = CLASS.ClassID; give an error?
options: Two tables can never be used in one query
ClassID is ambiguous because it is present in both tables
quiz.explain: A column name found in both tables must be qualified, e.g. STUDENT.ClassID or S.ClassID.
quiz.mistake: Does not realise the select list also needs qualified names

quiz.q: Which query is an equi-join using JOIN ... ON?
options: SELECT * FROM STUDENT JOIN CLASS ON STUDENT.ClassID = CLASS.ClassID;
quiz.explain: JOIN ... ON with an equality on the common column is an equi-join. SELECT * FROM STUDENT, CLASS; (and, in MySQL, JOIN without ON) gives a plain Cartesian product.
quiz.mistake: Mistakes a Cartesian product for a join

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): In an equi-join of STUDENT and CLASS on ClassID, the ClassID column appears twice in the output of SELECT *.
Reason (R): A natural join shows the common column only once.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both statements are true, but R describes a natural join; it does not explain why an equi-join shows the column twice (because SELECT * takes every column of both tables).
quiz.mistake: Takes a true statement about natural joins as the reason for equi-join behaviour

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If table A has 3 rows and table B has 4 rows, how many rows are in their Cartesian product, and why?'
teach.praise: Perfect! Each of A's 3 rows pairs with each of B's 4 rows, so there are 3 × 4 = 12 rows.
teach.nudge: How many partners does each row of A get from B, and what do you multiply?
